prompt.context: Midwest Hospital is a research-based hospital and takes pride in its joint replacement surgery department. Recently Midwest Hospital did a P&L analysis for all departments and found that the joint replacement surgery department is providing losses. The CEO has asked us to help out.
prompt.question: What is causing the losses in the joint replacement surgery department, and what should Midwest Hospital do to return the department to profitability?

clarifying_info.q: Are there any specific financial targets we need to hit?
clarifying_info.a: No, there are no financial targets.

clarifying_info.q: Should we consider other departments or only joint replacement surgery?
clarifying_info.a: The focus of this case is only on joint replacement surgery.

exhibits.title: Patient Mix
exhibits.shows: A table breaking down joint replacement surgeries by payer type, showing number of surgeries and pricing for each payer category.

exhibits.title: Joint Replacement Department P&L
exhibits.shows: A P&L statement for the joint replacement surgery department showing revenue, variable costs (broken out by physician, materials, and other), fixed costs (facilities and other), total costs, and profit.

exhibits.title: Competitive Benchmark
exhibits.shows: A competitive benchmark table comparing Midwest Hospital against four competitors on number of surgeries, patient mix by payer type (Commercial, HMO/Insurance, Medicare), and whether each is profitable.

framework: Revenues: Number of surgeries × price per surgery (varies by payer type); also post-surgery services (visits, medicines)
Revenue drivers: patient mix (commercial vs. insurance vs. Medicare), complexity of surgery, other charges (bed, medicines)
Costs — Fixed: hospital facilities, doctors, equipment, insurance, licenses
Costs — Variable: visiting doctors/surgeons, materials, government regulation compliance
Competition: pricing benchmarks, patient mix of competitors, quality/facilities
Customers: age group, insurance coverage type

questions.prompt: Exhibit 1: Would it be advisable to stop catering to Medicare patients (assume no backlash)?
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate the contribution margin per Medicare patient and compare to variable cost. Even if Medicare patients are unprofitable on a fully allocated basis, they still generate positive contribution margin above variable cost, helping cover fixed costs. Therefore it is not recommended to eliminate Medicare patients.

math.setup: Total surgeries = 1000. Revenue = Commercial (100 × $40K) + Insurance (300 × $20K) + Medicare (600 × $15K). VC = $14M total / 1000 surgeries = $14K per surgery. Contribution margin per Medicare patient = $15K – $14K = $1K.
steps: Total VC: $5M + $5M + $4M = $14M for 1,000 surgeries → $14K per surgery
Medicare invoiced price per patient = $15K; VC per patient = $14K
Eliminating Medicare patients removes $600K in contribution margin, worsening the loss
math.answer: Do NOT eliminate Medicare patients. Each Medicare surgery contributes $1K above variable cost toward covering $7M in fixed costs. Dropping 600 Medicare patients would reduce contribution by $600K and increase losses.

questions.prompt: Exhibit 2: What is the number of surgeries Midwest needs to conduct in a year to break even?
questions.guidance: Candidate should derive average revenue per patient and average variable cost per patient from Exhibit 1 and Exhibit 2, calculate gross margin per patient, then divide total fixed costs by gross margin per patient. Then break down the required mix using the same proportions.

math.setup: Average revenue = Total revenue / Total surgeries. Average VC = Total VC / Total surgeries. Gross margin per patient = Avg Rev – Avg VC. Breakeven surgeries = Fixed Costs / Gross margin per patient.
steps: Total revenue = $19M; Total surgeries = 1,000 → Average revenue per patient = $19M / 1,000 = $19K
Total VC = $14M; Total surgeries = 1,000 → Average VC per patient = $14M / 1,000 = $14K
Patient mix at same proportions (10% Commercial, 30% Insurance, 60% Medicare): Commercial = 140, Insurance = 420, Medicare = 840
math.answer: Midwest Hospital needs 1,400 surgeries per year to break even, requiring approximately 140 commercial, 420 insurance, and 840 Medicare patients (same 10/30/60 mix).

questions.prompt: Exhibit 3: Why is Company D able to stay profitable despite having fewer patients and a less favorable patient mix (75% Medicare) than Midwest?
questions.guidance: Candidate should recognize that Comp D has a similar or worse patient mix than Midwest (75% Medicare vs. 60%) and the same number of surgeries (1,000), yet is profitable. This points to a cost advantage, not a revenue advantage. Strong candidates identify that Comp D likely has a lower cost structure or negotiates better reimbursement rates from payers.

math.setup: Qualitative analysis — compare Comp D's profile to Midwest's profile.
steps: Comp D: 1,000 surgeries, 5% commercial / 25% HMO / 75% Medicare — profitable
Midwest: 1,000 surgeries, 10% commercial / 30% HMO / 60% Medicare — unprofitable
Comp D has MORE Medicare patients (75% vs 60%), so revenue mix is worse
Revenue advantage is unlikely given worse payer mix
Therefore Comp D must have lower variable or fixed costs, or better-negotiated reimbursement rates
math.answer: Comp D likely has a lower cost structure (lower VC per surgery and/or lower FC) or has negotiated better reimbursement rates from payers, allowing it to remain profitable with an even higher proportion of Medicare patients than Midwest.

brainstorming.prompt: Evaluate the potential risks to increasing the number of surgeries as a lever to reach breakeven.

categories.name: Market demand constraints
ideas: There may not be enough market demand to sustain 1,400 surgeries annually
Increasing volume would require stealing market share from competitors

categories.name: Competitive response
ideas: Competitors may react by reducing prices, triggering a price war
Competing hospitals may invest in facilities or marketing to protect volume

categories.name: Operational and quality risks
ideas: Scaling up quickly may strain capacity, staff, and equipment
Quality of care may decline with higher volume if resources are not added

categories.name: Regulatory and payer risks
ideas: Government may scrutinize a surge in Medicare-covered joint replacements
Insurance payers may renegotiate contracts if volumes shift significantly

recommendation: Increase total number of patients to cover the $7M in fixed costs — breakeven requires 1,400 surgeries (vs. current 1,000)
Shift patient mix toward higher-paying commercial and insurance patients to raise average revenue per surgery
Explore cost reduction through competitive benchmarking, targeting Comp D's apparent cost structure advantage
Do not eliminate Medicare patients — they still contribute positive margin above variable cost
Consider offering post-surgery services (physiotherapy, follow-up visits) as additional revenue streams
The joint replacement department may also serve as a loss leader that drives referrals and synergies with other departments — factor this into the profitability assessment
risks: Insufficient market demand to grow from 1,000 to 1,400 surgeries
Competitors may retaliate with price cuts if Midwest aggressively pursues commercial/insurance patients
Operational capacity constraints when scaling volume
Inability to negotiate lower costs with suppliers or payers in the short term
next_steps: Analyze scope for cost reduction through competitive benchmarking against Comp D
Analyze scope for price increase through competitive benchmarking
Start conversations with reimbursement providers (insurance companies and government) to negotiate better rates
Analyze profitability of post-care services (physiotherapy, follow-up)
Assess whether the department provides synergies with other hospital departments that offset the reported loss
